title: Ganglion
description: Clusters of neurons in the peripheral nervous system
wiki_lead:
A ganglion (pl.: ganglia) is a group of neuron cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system. In the somatic nervous system, this includes dorsal root ganglia and trigeminal ganglia among a few others. In the autonomic nervous system, there are both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia which contain the cell bodies of postganglionic sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons respectively.
A pseudoganglion looks like a ganglion, but only has nerve fibers and has few nerve cell bodies.
The restriction of the ganglion to refer to structures in the peripheral nervous system postdates the naming of brain structures such as the basal ganglia, which has remained as a historical artifact in vertebrate terminology. Among invertebrates the restriction is disregarded: for example, the main part of the insect brain is called the cerebral ganglion.
wiki_fulltext:
A ganglion (pl.: ganglia) is a group of neuron cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system. In the somatic nervous system, this includes dorsal root ganglia and trigeminal ganglia among a few others. In the autonomic nervous system, there are both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia which contain the cell bodies of postganglionic sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons respectively.
A pseudoganglion looks like a ganglion, but only has nerve fibers and has few nerve cell bodies.
The restriction of the ganglion to refer to structures in the peripheral nervous system postdates the naming of brain structures such as the basal ganglia, which has remained as a historical artifact in vertebrate terminology. Among invertebrates the restriction is disregarded: for example, the main part of the insect brain is called the cerebral ganglion.


Structure
Ganglia are primarily made up of somata and dendritic structures, which are bundled or connected. Ganglia often interconnect with other ganglia to form a complex system of ganglia known as a plexus. Ganglia provide relay points and intermediary connections between different neurological structures in the body, such as the peripheral and central nervous systems.
Among vertebrates there are three major groups of ganglia:

Dorsal root ganglia (also known as the spinal ganglia) contain the cell bodies of sensory (afferent) neurons.
Cranial nerve ganglia contain the cell bodies of cranial nerve neurons.
Autonomic ganglia contain the cell bodies of autonomic nerves.
In the autonomic nervous system, fibers from the central nervous system to the ganglia are known as preganglionic fibers, while those from the ganglia to the effector organ are called postganglionic fibers.


Basal ganglia
The term "ganglion" refers to the peripheral nervous system.
However, in the brain (part of the central nervous system), the basal ganglia are a group of nuclei interconnected with the cerebral cortex, thalamus, and brainstem, associated with a variety of functions: motor control, cognition, emotions, and learning.
Partly due to this ambiguity, the Terminologia Anatomica recommends using the term 'basal nuclei' instead of 'basal ganglia'; however, this usage has not been generally adopted.


Pseudoganglion
A pseudoganglion is a localized thickening of the main part or trunk of a nerve that has the appearance of a ganglion but has only nerve fibers and no nerve cell bodies.
Pseudoganglia are found in the teres minor muscle and radial nerve.
grok_lead: A ganglion is a localized cluster of neuronal cell bodies, typically found in the peripheral nervous system (PNS), serving as a site for processing or relaying neural signals outside the central nervous system (CNS). These structures are essential components of both the somatic and autonomic divisions of the PNS, where they house the soma (cell bodies) of neuron s that transmit sensory information or coordinate involuntary functions such as heart rate and digestion. Unlike the CNS, where neuron cell bodies are dispersed within gray matter, ganglia in the PNS form discrete, encapsulated nodules that facilitate efficient signal integration. Ganglia are broadly classified into sensory and autonomic types based on their function and location. Sensory ganglia, such as the dorsal root ganglia associated with spinal nerves, contain the cell bodies of pseudounipolar sensory neurons that convey afferent signals from peripheral receptors to the CNS; these are located just outside the spinal cord near the intervertebral foramina. Autonomic ganglia, in contrast, are involved in the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous systems, acting as relay points where preganglionic fibers synapse with postganglionic neurons; examples include prevertebral ganglia such as the celiac ganglion, which regulates visceral organs. In vertebrates, ganglia vary in size from microscopic clusters to larger aggregates like the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve, which supports sensory and motor functions of the face. Notable aspects of ganglia include their role in neurological disorders; for instance, damage to dorsal root ganglia can lead to neuropathic pain due to disrupted sensory processing. Additionally, while the term "ganglion" traditionally refers to PNS structures, it is sometimes extended to CNS nuclei like the basal ganglia, a group of subcortical nuclei involved in motor control and reward pathways, though these lack the peripheral encapsulation. In non-vertebrate animals, such as insects, ganglia form segmental components of a ventral nerve cord, highlighting evolutionary conservation in neural organization.
